argument_summary: The admissible record supports certification as a weak, caveated readiness judgment rather than a clean policy-compliance showing. Aggregate readiness clears by 2.0 percentage points and the launch rehearsal had no severity-one incidents, which supports general launch readiness. Public governance guidance also supports documenting limitations and managing risk through ongoing measurement and monitoring across deployment. The narrower claim is that certification is supportable if treated as conditioned on explicit acknowledgment of the named-segment limitation, not that the current record proves the issue is immaterial or already fully satisfied under policy.
claims_about_business_cost: Escalation is not required by the admissible record if the auditor can distinguish between rejecting clean compliance and treating the packet as a caveated certification basis. General readiness evidence is positive, and a no-severity-one rehearsal result reduces the case for treating the release as broadly unsafe. The remaining dispute is specific and bounded to the named segment and disclosure treatment, so the cost of full escalation may be disproportionate if the packet is framed as limited support rather than full closure.
claims_about_policy: The current admissible record does not support claiming clean compliance with the disclosure policy. The policy text makes a weakness material when it affects a named launch use case, and the record shows the supply-chain vendor screening segment is named in two manufacturer rollout commitments. Product's non-core characterization informs prioritization but does not resolve materiality on this record. The best policy-grounded interpretation available is that certification can be defended only as caveated, because aggregate readiness evidence supports release readiness in general while the disclosure-or-risk-acceptance predicate remains unresolved.
concessions: The named-segment evaluation gap is real and currently misses target by 1.4 percentage points.
The affected segment is named in two manufacturer rollout commitments, which cuts against any claim of immateriality.
The legal disclosure question remains open on the current record.
Public model-card and monitoring guidance does not by itself satisfy the internal requirement for disclosure, resolution, or approved risk acceptance before launch.
The current record does not support saying certification is cleanly policy-compliant without caveat.
